results.summary: This design is a metastability characterization circuit that generates metastability by sampling a locally generated asynchronous data signal. A metastability detector observes the sampled signals and identifies events, with two selectable detector implementations. A tunable delay adjusts the effective metastability resolution window so events persisting beyond that window can be detected. The selected detector output is counted to provide a measurable indication of metastability activity.

results.summary: This project renders a full-screen animated XOR plasma effect on a VGA display at 640x480 resolution and 60 Hz, using a 25 MHz pixel clock. It is authored in Spade HDL and compiled to SystemVerilog before synthesis. Eight input pins provide real-time controls for pause, pattern select, speed, colour inversion and colour rotation. results.summary: This design computes a 4-element dot product in GF16 format, using four parallel combinational GF16 multipliers and three GF16 adders in a tree reduction. The GF16 format has 1 sign bit, 6 exponent bits with bias 31, and 9 mantissa bits. By default it computes dot4([1,2,3,4],[1,2,3,4]) = 30.0 = 0x47C0, observable as uo_out = 0xC0 and uio_out = 0x47. No external hardware is required, and the result is directly observable on the output pins.

results.summary_before: This design implements a host-driven primitive engine for transformer layers, featuring a 2x2 systolic array of multiply-accumulate processing elements with signed 5-bit operands and 11-bit results. The interface allows a host to write operands and commands, and read results one word at a time. No external hardware is required beyond a standard Tiny Tapeout board or simulator, and the design is notable for its compact implementation of a systolic schedule.
results.summary: This design is a host-driven primitive engine for transformer layers, built around a fixed signed 2x2 systolic array of multiply-accumulate processing elements. The A and B banks store signed 5-bit operands, while the C bank stores signed 11-bit results wide enough for the exact sum of two signed 5-bit products. A host writes operands and commands through the interface and reads one stored word at a time via a small addressable read mux. No external hardware is required beyond a normal Tiny Tapeout board or simulator host.
